#8355. The Dump Truckers: Behind the Tramily Name

I awoke in our tent at the Muskrat Creek Shelter to the sound of birds chirping. Through the open flap of my vestibule I could see nothing but a wall of green rhododendron and gray fog. Yet another late winter misty morning in the Appalachians.

The climb up Standing Indian Mountain was kind to us, offering a gradual incline. Nearing the top we walked across a spooky, socked-in ridgeline. Beige dead grasses and deep crimson bare branches of a leafless shrub lined the dirt trail. Above us the fog tangled eerily in crooked branches of naked trees. The summit offered no views. We only knew we’d reached it because of the sign.

Later in the day I saw another sign: the first indication that spring was coming. The tiniest blue flowers, no bigger than my pinky nail. Called azure bluets (also known as Quaker ladies), these are indeed classified as “spring ephemerals.” They’re wildflowers that bloom early in the season, capitalizing on the additional sunlight before the trees grow their summer canopy.

As Show and I walked with Leigh, a North Carolina native, she pointed out another local plant to us. Growing alongside the trail was a low-growing, leafy plant with maroon heart-shaped leaves. “This is called galax,” she informed us. Typically this plant is green in color, but we were now seeing it with it’s cold weather and sun defenses up. A shade dweller, galax produces red and purple anthocyanin pigments in the winter to both protect it from excess sunlight due to the bare trees but also to help with absorbing additional light energy while the sun is weaker.

If anyone reading this was on trail behind us this year, it’s possible you noticed the name “Dump Truckers” signed in a log book here and there. Or noticed a comment thread inviting you to participate in a “Dump Truck Challenge” on FarOut’s Albert Mountain waypoint. Maybe you thought, what’s with this dump truck stuff? Well, here’s the backstory.

To explain this I have to take it back to my thru-hike of the Pacific Crest Trail in 2023. Anyone who’s hiked the PCT northbound may remember a challenge of the same name posted to the Washington FarOut map. Essentially, it’s an unofficial time trial tradition that thru-hikers complete to put their 2,400 miles worth of trail legs to the test. We call it this because the grueling climb requires immense effort from your glutes, also known as your ass, also known as your “dump truck.” Roughly 700 feet of elevation over 0.7 miles up a steep pitch between Snoqualmie and Stevens Passes. That’s where the challenge originates, as far as I’m concerned.

Spectacle Lake in Washington on the PCT, located just a few trail miles south of the DTC. Photo taken on my 2023 thru-hike.

For whatever unremembered reason, Show and I recalled this challenge as we approached Albert Mountain in North Carolina. This mountain has significance because its summit is the 100 mile marker of the Appalachian Trail northbound. An idea sparked: what if we brought the Dump Truck Challenge to the Appalachian Trail?

Why we decided to implement this at merely mile 100 versus over 2,000 is neither here nor there. The timing was coincidental, not impeccable. We wanted something special to commemorate having hiked our first 100 miles and this turned out to be the thing. And in our defense, the AT DTC is theoretically easier because it’s shorter: only 0.3 miles up, a little under 400 feet. How bad could it be?

Can you spot the Albert Mountain fire tower through the trees?

In comparison to the one on the PCT? Bad. At least for me.

Show started first, taking off at a rather quick pace from the bottom of the first steps by the last road crossing before the summit and fire tower, the trial’s official starting line, as established by us. I waited a bit at that first stair to leave some distance between us, not that it was necessary. I was fairly certain I wouldn’t catch him. But just in case.

I went next. Plugging into my earbuds with some upbeat music on, I clicked the button on my watch to start the timer. Foolishly, I gave into the adrenaline coursing through my body and pushed off at far too fast a clip. About halfway up I was already gassed, having paced it incorrectly. I’m a bit ashamed to admit I more or less gave up and walked the rest of the hill at my normal pace, gasping for air, sweat pouring down my face. Nearing the top I picked it up to a half-hearted hustle for the last 100 feet or so to the firetower: the finish line.

I tagged the metal scaffolding at 9 minutes 37 seconds. Show had smoked me with his time of 7 minutes 25 seconds. I didn’t let the results bother me. It was so early on in the trail that it was unreasonable expect a challenge like this would come easy. Besides, it was all in good fun, not about the score.

Leigh, Noah, and Cous Cous each arrived at the fire tower not long behind us, finishing their DTCs in 7 minutes 40 seconds, 7 minutes 47 seconds, and 9 minutes 22 seconds, respectively. Everyone was beat physically, but feeling rewarded mentally for having completed the challenge and reached 100 miles!

“I’m putting a comment on FarOut, what should I say?” Show asked me. We wanted to see if others behind us would do the Dump Truck Challenge. For the one on the PCT, it’s customary to comment “Dump Truck Challenge” followed by your trail name and time for everyone to see.

“Hmmm,” I thought aloud. “How about… how fast can you blast your ass?”

Looking back months later, I’m proud to report that quite a few hikers have completed the DTC since March! It’s kind of a thing now, and it’s cool to think we started it. Hopefully the tradition continues for seasons to come. So if you’re planning to do the AT in a future year, make sure you blast your ass up Albert and comment your time on FarOut. Let’s keep this going!

Reaching the 100 mile marker called for a group photo. Those of us who were there at the time gathered by the railing of Albert’s scenic overlook. I set up my tripod, coiling its bendy legs around the scaffolding of the fire tower, and trotted back over to snap the photo.

It wasn’t the only picture taken. I have no memory of who actually said it (perhaps Show, that would track), but one of us cheekily suggested we take another, this time mooning the camera. Afterall, we had busted our butts to tag this mile marker… After some coy protests from Cous Cous, some mild peer pressure, and an eventual giving-in, the five of us turned around and exposed our bare asses.

I’ve put a lot of thought into if and how I want to share photos of this nature online. It wouldn’t be such a big deal if this were a one time thing. But the “butts out” photos, as our tramily referred to them, kind of became A Thing. A tradition we carried on throughout the entire trail, that commemorated every 100 miles we hiked. It was a significant part of our tramily culture. And we got quite creative with them as time went on, selecting specific locales and picking our poses. In a way it feels wrong to exclude them entirely, like I’d be omitting a huge plotline in the story. It was one of the things that made our tramily ours.

The problem here is that I do not have explicit consent to post said explicit photos from everyone featured in them. In fact, I’m actually under strict orders from one person NOT to post them online.

So here’s what I’m going to do. Firstly, I have been and I’m going to continue to keep them off of social media (Instagram, YouTube) entirely. The only place they will be posted are here on The Trek. You’ll get glimpses of my thru-hikes elsewhere, but you have to be willing to read the blog if you want the full and complete story. That’s how I’ve always operated with my online trail content. So it will be an intimate part of the story only my readers will get to know. (Y’all are my favorites. Don’t tell the folks on the other platforms that.)

Secondly, I’m going to blur the butts (and in one case, that person entirely). You’ll still be able to tell it’s a “butts out” picture because you’ll see it enough, but it will be pixelated so not to reveal any fine detail. Thirdly, I’m only going to post the photos that include me. There were a few times when the tramily was on slightly different schedules and took separate butts out photos as we individually reached those mile markers. There needs to be the autovulnerability of my own mild nudity occurring with this. Lastly, I will never caption the photo with who is in it. Most of the time our faces aren’t included anyway. This will allow for a tad more anonymity.

Most importantly, I’ve also directly asked everyone who is featured in more than just one or two of these photos for their consent to post the censored versions on the blog. They were all appreciative of being asked first and have consented. So without further preface, below is our first ever butts out tramily photo!

I can’t remember exactly when, but it was sometime between this photo and the following couples days when we were in the town of Franklin, North Carolina that we began calling ourselves “The Dump Truckers.” It referred to both the Dump Truck Challenge and the butts out photo, which really were one and the same reference. I do remember gathering everyone’s phone numbers and adding them to a group chat with that name. We called ourselves this for quite awhile—over half of the trail. It was only after losing a long-term original member that we felt it was best to rebrand the band. That’s all the blatant foreshadowing you’ll get on that for now.

Show and I spent the next couple days and nights surrounded by the most other hikers we’d been around yet. The whole crew from Muskrat Creek Shelter and then some were moving at about the same pace we were. One afternoon, a few miles shy of camp, a whole group of us including myself, Show, Noah, Leigh, Cous Cous, Alex, Braxton, and Bill stopped at a rhododendron-canopied stream to “soak the dogs.”

We pulled off our shoes and socks, switched into camp shoes (or simply bare feet) and stuck our aching, barely broken-in feet into the frigid water. Braxton didn’t even bother to remove his trail runners, instead doing a “full shoe soak” as he called it. It was a fun memory of everyone gathered together, resting and chatting and laughing, all on the same but simultaneously separate journeys.

The night before our second town stop in Franklin, North Carolina the whole crew camped at Rock Gap Shelter, less than 4 miles south of Winding Stair Gap, our exit point for Franklin. All those mentioned in the previous paragraph were there, and then some. Rewind, a mid-50s man named Pantry who we’d briefly met once or twice without proper introduction, and a few others I never formally met all showed up for the night.

As I was collecting water in our CNOC from the piped spring on the side of the shelter, Pantry came over and introduced himself. “I heard you guys are from New Hampshire?” he confirmed, “I am too, actually. Well, unfortunately I live in fucking Mass right now, but I still like to say New Hampshire.” His heavy Boston accent and liberal use of the F-bomb would have pinpointed him definitively to either of those states without him directly name-dropping them.

He was the first other New Englander we’d met out there. Most of the others were from the south, midwest, or various other parts of the country. I also learned from this brief exchange that Pantry, like me, was a repeat offender. He had already thru-hiked the AT in 2019, the year before my first thru. I knew via reading pre-hike Trek blogs that there was going to be at least one other second-timer out there this season (shout out to Nor’easter) but here was another. It surprised me that there were even three of us like-minded hikers that were willing to do this whole thing twice.

Show and I also got to know Alex a bit better by hanging out with him at the Rock Gap shelter. As the dreads, face tat, and watermelon fanny had indicated, he was indeed an interesting character. Since that first interaction when he’d dejectedly told us he’d see us at Katahdin, he’d gotten a trail name: Rufio.

If you’re familiar with the ’90s movie Hook, a spin-off of the Peter Pan story starring Robin Williams and Julia Roberts, you’ll immediately get the reference. At the time, I didn’t get it, because I hadn’t seen the movie. But since returning home from the trail, I have watched the movie on high recommendation from Rufio and as research for the blog. If, like me, you’re not familiar, Rufio’s character is the de facto leader of the Lost Boys in Neverland. He and the gang of forever-kids frequently shout “Bangarang!” as a sort of battle cry to rally the troops or simply an ecstatic expression of wild joy. So that’s who I heard shouting at the state line the other day, I put two and two together in my mind.

The name and meaning behind it were certainly fitting. It was evident that Rufio (Alex, not the character) fully embraces Neverland’s “never grow up” mindset. And NOT in a Peter Pan syndrome way, implying he’s immature and rejects adulting. In a good way: he’s a person who lives big and bold, refusing to lose touch with his childlike playfulness and whimsy no matter how old he gets.

Throughout the time I spent with Rufio he mentioned more than once that he never thought he’d live to be as old as he was. Born a few months before me in the fall of 1990, he was also 35. He revealed on this night at the Rock Gap shelter that he’d had a tumultuous past including times of drug addiction and drug-related incarceration. Thirty-five might not seem like a ripe old age to the average person, but that’s pushing 60 in addict years. Heavy drug users such as many of the famous musicians in the so-called “27 Club” don’t even make it to their thirties. Knowing this, I completely understood why he connects so strongly with the forever young trope in Peter Pan and Hook.

Hearing some of Rufio’s stories, I considered revealing that I’m also an addict—but didn’t, not yet anyway. I’m not entirely sure why it is, but I still feel squirmy outing myself as sober to new people. Even four years into sobriety. I’d imagined that this uncomfortability would have diminished by now, but the reality is that it hasn’t. Maybe I’m simply out of practice. I don’t “work a program” like AA where I’m repeatedly finding myself in a room full of people proclaiming that “my name is Kelly and I’m an alcoholic.” Nor do I have many sober friends or acquaintances in real life (though I interact casually with a few online).

That may be part of it, but the squirminess has deeper roots. In Shame. While I’m extremely proud of all the progress I’ve made in my recovery journey, simultaneously, the shameful beliefs about my past self still linger. Honestly, that decade of drinking feels, in hindsight, like it was not only a lifetime ago, but another person’s life entirely. Like I got transported into another body and mind for awhile. Now I’m back, scratching my head going, what the fuck was THAT? Like waking up from a bizarre nightmare.

If you knew me in my drinking days (my apologies, first off) I was wild, loud and obnoxious, and unpresent. Now, I still identify as being wild, in a different sense. I’m naturally more quiet and reserved, down-to-earth. There’s a glaring disconnect between these two identities that’s hard for me to reconcile. I worry I now present so clean-cut and (mostly) mild-mannered that people, particularly other addicts, won’t believe me when I claim the label. Especially that they’ll hit me with the “you don’t look/seem like an alcoholic…” or “I never would have guessed…” which will trigger the shame spiral of: why the hell did I end up this way? Someone like me shouldn’t have ended up this way.

Personally, I got a lot of my former “spunkiness” from the booze. It doesn’t feel like an organic part of me that was exacerbated by the drink. Whereas, for whatever reason, I perceive that other addicts innately always had that spunk and carry it over into sobriety, shamelessly making others laugh with their war stories. I just feel awkward and pathetic telling mine, so I usually don’t. Here I go again with the imposter syndrome. Jeez, I can’t even positively embrace a “negative” identity. I’m a real addict, too! I swear! Ridiculous, haha.

I’ll close out this tangent by saying that I hope to someday loosen the tight grip of shame and take comfortable ownership of my spunky past in front of others more. I’m sure like a lot of things it will take time and practice, apparently more than I’d bargained for. I greatly envy those that espouse sobriety shame-free. Not the case for this alcoholic.

Why is it named this? Who named it? We may never know.

Why is toileting being encouraged in this one specific area? The fact that this was fairly close to a stream was the most alarming part.

Now that I’ve added these photos, I suppose I have SOME sober spunk. I do have my Silly Goose Certification, a prestigious honor I don’t take lightly.

In addition to finding out Rufio’s recently claimed trail name, another one unfolded in real time around the picnic table that night at dinner. Braxton had pulled out a quart-sized Ziploc of single use sauce and condiment packets, the kind you get a fast food restaurants. The bag was stuffed to the brim with all varieties, from McDonald’s mustard to Taco Bell Fire Sauce to soy sauce from Asian restaurants. Someone commented, “damn dude, that’s a lot of sauce packets!”

“Your trail name should be Sauce Packet,” I suggested.

“I mean,” Braxton added, “I have been saving up all of these for like two years…”

Everyone laughed. The time-effort that had gone into collecting the packets pre-hike solidified it. The name quickly got shortened to just “Sauce,” which I approved of. “Sauce” has a nice clean, bold ring to it. Being present for a trail name origin story is one of my favorite things on a thru-hike. I love watching a core memory play out; the instant it clicks that an initially random moment will be anecdotally significant for this person. A tale they’ll tell over and over again whenever asked about their trail name. It’s exciting to witness someone who doesn’t yet have one click with and accept their trail identity. I love it.

Embracing my toddler snacks identity in the baby food aisle of Vons in Mammoth Lakes, CA on the PCT.

I don’t know if it’s just me and my group that did this, but occasionally we’d give someone a private trail name. As I’ve mentioned in previous blogs, this was the case with the guys I called “First Cathole” and “Snorlax.” We never saw them again beyond the first week, so I have no idea if they ended up getting official trail names or even completed the trail. But my names for them are a way to refer to someone whose name I never knew, but also in memoriam of those first funny interactions with them.

Not long after Sauce accepted his new name, another woman we didn’t know was cutting cheese. In the literal sense. “Does anyone want any?” she offered to the masses, “I packed out way too much.”

“I do!” Cous Cous exclaimed, always accepting of any and all free food.

The woman cut him a slice with her pocket knife and reached out to hand it over. Unfortunately, the transfer got fumbled and the cheese slice dropped to the dirt. “Oh no,” she said hurriedly, “don’t eat that, I’ll cut you another.”

Before anyone knew what was happening, she started pounding the reject cheese into the ground under her trailrunner. Surprisingly it didn’t automatically disappear as a result of this brute force action, it only got flatter and dirtier. Great, I thought, now we’ve got cheese ten feet away from the shelter where we’re sleeping… I made a mental note to circle back and scrape it off the ground and put it in my trash bag before we all went to bed. I felt weird doing so in the moment, like I was presenting “holier-than-thou” or something by doing the right thing and packing it out.

Debriefing on this later once the woman wasn’t in the vicinity, I discovered I wasn’t the only one that disagreed with her cheese disposal method. We all agreed it was not only NOT LNT, but quite strange, and began referring to her from then on as “Cheese Stomper.”

“I would have still eaten it if she hadn’t stomped all over it!” Cous Cous sighed, shaking his head at the thought of five-second-rule-perfectly-good food gone to waste.

We didn’t see CS again for a very long time, but months later eventually ran into her somewhere in Pennsylvania. I honestly didn’t recognize her (still wouldn’t if I saw her on the street) but after seeing her again Leigh reminded me, “you know who that was?? Cheese Stomper!”

As the sky was fading to black, the Lost Boys (Rufio, Show, Noah, Cous Cous, and I) settled down into our sleeping bags in the shelter. The night was mild and still. All of the good vibes from the evening’s hang hung in the air. It relaxed me to be in nature, in good company. Rufio inhaled one last hit off his bowl and exhaled a cloud into the darkness, illuminated lime green in the beam of his headlamp. “Goodnight, Neverland!” he spoke serenely into the night.

#8353. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#8350. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind

The main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

There are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

His article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”

A recent study showed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

There is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

In a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

The review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind

The other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949

What exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

Clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how big they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

The area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he shows to the world.”

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8348. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

There is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

The one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman said. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two new routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman says this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

At the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.)

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment issues, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

In the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman

Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#8346. Congratulations to These 2026 Pacific Crest Trail Finishers (Part 7)

The Pacific Crest Trail is one of North America’s most beautiful and iconic thru-hikes, stretching 2,650 miles from the Mexican border all the way to Canada. Every year, thousands of hikers set out on this unforgettable journey, pushing their limits both physically and mentally as they navigate this incredibly diverse terrain.

This year, wildfires devastated many thru-hikers’ plans. In July, the northern section of the PCT from Harts Pass to the Canadian border was closed due to the Ptarmigan Fire. Because of this, many finish photos look different than in years past.

Thru-hiking teaches lessons in perseverance and resilience, and many hikers were able to pivot from a traditional finish and found creative conclusions to their multi-month journey before the northern terminus officially reopened in mid-September. We’re thrilled to spotlight the incredible hikers who completed this journey in 2026, no matter the end point!

Have you just finished your PCT thru-hike? If so, please celebrate your finish with us by submitting a photo through the form below so we can feature you in a subsequent post. We can’t wait to share your incredible achievement!

“Hopped off trail at White Pass while the fire closures and smoke were still present- I’ll be coming back next year to do the rest!” -Meadowlark

“After fires closed us off from the PCT at Snoqualmie Pass, and with no desire to road walk or inhale smoke any longer, we sent it to the Olympics for a 160-mile traverse, ending along the wilderness coast, making our northern terminus the Strait of Juan de Fuca – the water border with Canada!” -Two Plates

“Found love on the PCT! The trail provides 🫶🏻” -Sunflower & Just Nick

“Despite the difficulties towards the end of the hike, all I can say it was awesome.” -Willem

“PCT was everything I’d ever dreamed of and much more. Even though it once seemed so unachievable, here I am. As a note to my future self, I’d like to keep in mind that even what seems impossible can become reality if you just dare to go for it. You can become anyone. You can do anything. Don’t wait for a better opportunity. Don’t wait for your future self to feel better prepared. Do it now. And while doing it, cherish every moment. Because once lived through, it will be gone forever.” -Freedom

“If you’re going through hell, just keep going.” -Lipstick

Congratulations to all the 2026 PCT finishers — your achievements are remarkable and worth celebrating!

#8341. Sweeping New BLM Proposal Would Limit Public Comment and Weaken Environmental Protections for American West

Following a year of attempted sweeping changes to US public land management, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) has proposed a rewrite of some of the most foundational regulations for managing more than 245 million acres of public land across the American West that would limit public comment and reduce environmental reviews.

Published on November 10 in the Federal Register, the proposal would overhaul how the agency plans projects, seeks public input, and adheres to environmental rules. Officially titled Revision of Regulations for Planning, Programming, Budgeting (43 CFR Part 1600), the BLM’s proposed changes would arguably be the largest overhaul of these rules since their adoption in 1979 under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act.

Officials from the Department of the Interior claim these revisions will accelerate project approvals, while local communities and conservation groups argue that the proposal would strip environmental safeguards to fast-track oil and gas drilling, mining, and commercial development.

One of the most important changes in the BLM’s proposal is the removal of the requirement that the agency prepare a comprehensive Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) each time it writes or revises a Resource Management Plan. These resource plans determine where extraction, grazing, recreation, and conservation can occur on public lands, and an EIS evaluates them for potential harm to ecosystems and surrounding communities.

Doug Burgum has served as the United States Secretary of the Interior since February 1, 2025. Photo via Doug Burgum

In the proposal, the regulatory section previously titled “Environmental Impact Statement” would be renamed “Environmental Compliance,” and the automatic EIS requirement would be removed, instead allowing the BLM “to determine how best to comply with NEPA during land use planning.” The agency claims that the current requirement duplicates procedures already governed by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

Alongside the changes to environmental reviews, the proposal substantially limits the ability of the public and partner governments to weigh in. The rule eliminates the mandatory 90-day public comment period for draft land-use plans and EISs and replaces it with a 30-day window that can be extended by no more than 30 additional days.

It also removes requirements to publish a Federal Register notice when launching a planning process and drops the 30-day comment period previously required when the agency makes major last-minute changes to a proposed plan. Notably, the proposal would also enable BLM to replace written public comment periods with public meetings “when permissible under other authorities — such as NEPA — and when adequate notice to the public is provided.”

At the intergovernmental level, the proposal ends the requirement that BLM land-use plans maintain consistency with Tribal governments and other federal agency plans, while cutting a state governor’s final consistency review window from 60 days to 30 days and eliminating the governor’s right to appeal a rejection to the BLM Director. These changes strip away the legal leverage that Tribal nations, neighboring federal agencies, and state governors currently use to work with the BLM to align on land-use decisions.

The proposed rule would create a new regulatory mechanism entitled “Amending Land Use Plans To Address Emergencies” that would authorize a Senate-confirmed official in the Department of the Interior to bypass standard consultation procedures when amending a plan to support projects responding to “emergency circumstances.” However, the proposed text neither defines what constitutes an “emergency circumstance” nor limits the types of commercial or infrastructure projects that could qualify for the expedited track.

A map showing the land currently managed by the BLM. Photo via BLM

The proposal also overhauls how the BLM designates and manages Areas of Critical Environmental Concern (ACECs), which are landscapes recognized for sensitive fish and wildlife habitat, cultural sites, or natural hazards.

The new proposal removes requirements for a separate 60-day public comment period and Federal Register notice for proposed ACECs. Interior officials stated the revisions will give the agency greater flexibility to “right-size” designations rather than manage what the department described as “oversized buffer zones.”

“The boundaries of designated areas of critical environmental concern shall encompass the smallest area of public lands necessary to protect and prevent irreparable damage of the relevant and important values,” reads the proposal.

In a statement announcing the revisions, the BLM said the rule “would update planning terminology, eliminate duplicate requirements and simplify parts of the planning process that have become unnecessarily burdensome over time,” while ensuring public input occurs at “the most meaningful stages.”

Environmental advocacy organizations, including Earthjustice and the Sierra Club, condemned the proposal immediately following its release, arguing that eliminating mandatory EIS reviews and 90-day comment periods will allow the administration to make sweeping land-use decisions behind closed doors while sidelining local communities, Tribes, scientists, conservationists, and those who recreate on public lands.

The 60-day public comment period on the proposed rule (Docket No. BLM-2026-0298) is currently open through January 11, 2027. You can submit a public comment here. The BLM has also scheduled a virtual public information session for December 3, 2026.

Featured image: A BLM sign marking part of the Pacific Crest Trail. Photo: Nina Butler, 2025

#8339. Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

Published Nov 7, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I had just come back from the service in 1954. My wife was expecting our first baby, and I was running a general store on Highway 97 just outside of Bainbridge, Georgia. Hardly a day went by that someone didn’t come in and tell tales of Old Ripper.

Old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp. That hog tore up more fences, broke more gates, broke the backs of more female hogs and was chased by more hunters than any critter there has ever been in this country. Ripper had been shot by several people. My Daddy fired at him seven times with an M-1 carbine and believed he hit him, but the hog never fell. He had been hunted with dogs and he had killed plenty of dogs. There never was a hog hound that could hold him. The last time the boar was run with hounds, he killed two of the best hounds in the county with his slashing tusks, so no one else ever put their dogs on Old Ripper.

Old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy. Farmers around Bainbridge went to the hardware stores and bought brand-new aluminum gates to put in the gaps he made in their fences. Within a week, the gates were often all bent and torn up where that crazy boar had stuck his nose under and bent them to get into a pasture or field. There was no hog wire or barbed wire fence that could keep Old Ripper out.

That boar was walking destruction. The farmers hated him not only for tearing up fences and gates, but even more because of what he did to their sows. Ripper would break into a pig parlor, tear up the pens and release all the sows. Then he would take them off for a stroll in the woods. Old Ripper weighed 438 pounds. So when he mounted some of the young sows, he broke their backs. Then the sows would have to be destroyed. The sows he did breed threw shoats that were as wild and crazy as he was. The piglets wouldn’t fatten and brought almost nothing at the market.

Everybody was out to get Old Ripper. My dad was accustomed to catching wild hogs. We used to catch them in the Fowltown Swamp, fatten them and sell them at the market. My daddy knew about trapping hogs. He built traps to catch Old Ripper. On two separate occasions Old Ripper did go into one of daddy’s traps, but he tore up the wooden stockades and broke out both times. My daddy wouldn’t stand for that, so daddy got a steel bear trap and set it for Ripper. When daddy went back the next day he found the giant tracks of Old Ripper and followed them to the trap. But instead of catching a renegade hog, he found the bear trap had been sprung by the big boar.

One reason Old Ripper became a legend was his ability to outthink the farmers and the hunters in our area. He had been around humans so much that in many cases he just outthought folks instead of using brute force. The people around our place began to think Old Ripper might be a supernatural creature. He was a boar, but he was a smart boar. No dogs could hold him, no stockades could enclose him, no fence could stop him and no man had been able to kill him for seven years.

Other episodes added to the legend of Old Ripper. One of the meanest things Old Ripper ever did involved Mrs. Ella T. Hand’s daughter-in-law, who was five months pregnant. She was in her kitchen and heard a disturbance out among her sows. She went out to the pig parlor and saw Old Ripper trying to tear the planks off the posts where she had her sows penned up. She picked up a rock and threw it at the old boar to try and run him off. When he saw her, he turned, looked straight at her and charged. Only a few steps away was a giant red oak stump that stood about three feet off the ground. The lady climbed up on the stump and began to scream for her husband. All the while, Old Ripper was going around the stump, snorting and blowing. He attempted to rear up on that stump and get to her but she stayed just out of reach of his razor-sharp tusks. For an hour the hog circled the stump as the lady screamed for help. Finally her husband came home. When he saw what was happening, he grabbed his shotgun from over the fireplace and ran toward the hog. At less than 10 yards, he shot Old Ripper in the side of the head with birdshot. The hog merely shook his head, looked at the man and trotted off.

To say Old Ripper was hated by everybody in the community would be a vast understatement. Every man and boy dreamed of killing that old boar, and plenty of work was forgotten by the men who hunted him. All it took to organize a community hog hunt was for someone to report that they’d seen Old Ripper. Every man and boy within earshot would grab a gun and head for the swamp.

I would have liked to have hunted Old Ripper, but I had mouths to feed. I didn’t have time to waste on that renegade boar. I had just bought a brand-new lever-action Marlin .30/30. I was proud of that gun and took it out behind the store to test it out. On that particular day, Mrs. Ella T. Hand happened to be sitting out in front of the store. Mrs. Hand was close to 80 years old. She always wore a sunbonnet, a long dress and about 90 percent of the time, she had a dip of snuff in her mouth. Mrs. Hand saw me kill a crow sitting in the field about 150 yards away with that rifle. I knew I’d made a lucky shot, but she didn’t. She told everyone for a month about how good I could shoot with that new .30/30.

“If that old wild hog comes back around my sows, I’m going to come and get you, Jack, and let you kill him with that new rifle,” she told me.

Well, about a month later, here comes Mrs. Ella T. in her 1949 pickup truck.

“Jack, that old boar is up in my field with some sows he run off,” she told me. “Now I don’t expect you’ll have any better luck than anybody else who has tried to kill him, but I sure wish you’d bring that new rifle up to the field and give it a try.”

I closed up my little country store and got into the front seat of that pickup truck with Mrs. Ella T. to try my hand at Old Ripper. I had five cartridges with copper-jacketed lead-headed bullets in my gun—the kind that open up but still go on through. There wasn’t any doubt in my mind that if I could hit that boar, the bullets would do the damage needed to put him down.

We drove to Mrs. Hand’s 40-acre peanut field, which backed up to the edge of Fowltown Swamp. I saw Old Ripper out in the middle of the field with four sows he had just broken out from their pen. The five pigs were all rooting in the peanuts. There was a hog wire fence around the field, with barbed wire on the top. The field, which was about 250 yards wide and about twice as long, was on a hillside. Old Ripper and the sows were up close to the top of the hill and I was down near the bottom. There was a dried-up creekbed that ran under the fence. From the tracks in the wash, I figured this was where Old Ripper and the sows had gotten into the field. The creekbed was only about two or three feet deep, but it was big enough for me to crawl under the fence and still stay out of sight. I could lay down in the bottom of the wash, crawl along on my stomach and Old Ripper wouldn’t be able to see me.

Until that day, I had never seen Old Ripper. I had looked at fences he had torn up and I had seen mud on the sides of the trees where he had rubbed. I knew he was a big boar, but I never realized just how big. When I saw Old Ripper standing there in the sun, his black bristles gathered in the rays of light and made him look a deep royal blue. He was a magnificent animal standing about four feet high, and he completely dwarfed the sows following him.

I said to myself, “Doggone your hide, Old Ripper! I’m going to try and get a little closer to you.”

The wash meandered from the bottom of the slope where I was uphill to where Old Ripper was rooting in the peanut patch. Lying flat on my belly, I would crawl for 10 yards and then peep over the edge to see where Old Ripper was. Each time I looked, the old boar was about 10 yards farther from the place than he had been before. It was just like he had a sixth sense that warned him of danger. He kept the same distance away, about 230 yards from me, from the time I first saw him until I decided to shoot. After I had crawled 30 yards, Old Ripper and his band of runaway sows were within 10 yards of a thick broom sedge field. I knew that if he got into that field, I wouldn’t be able to see to shoot him.

The wash was shallower and just barely kept me out of the boar’s view. The shot had to be over 200 yards. So I laid the rifle down on the lip of the wash, looked through the open sights and aimed at the top of Old Ripper’s shoulder. When I squeezed off the first shot, I saw the dust fly off the boar’s shoulder and heard the bullet make a dull thud when it hit him, but Old Ripper showed no sign of being wounded.

Then I stood up. Old Ripper reared up on his hind legs and bellowed like a wild bull. The hair on the back of my neck stood up. I had caught or killed more than 100 hogs out of that swamp, but I had never heard a hog make a sound like that.

When Old Ripper came down on his front feet, he was on a dead run, headed right down that hill. I knew that when he got to the bottom of the hill, he had business with me. I should have killed Old Ripper with that first shot, but he was far from dead. I didn’t panic. I knew that before the boar got to me, I would have time to fire four more of those .30/30 shells. I thought there was no way I wouldn’t kill him before he got to me. I had faced other wild hogs before.

With every shot, I believed I was pumping more lead into Old Ripper, but he never slowed. He still came on toward me. I took my time, aimed, squeezed, heard the report of the rifle, jacked another shell into the chamber and fired again. I knew I was hitting the boar, but he never missed a stride.

When Old Ripper was less than 50 yards away, I heard the hammer fall on an empty chamber. That was the loudest, most desperate sound I ever heard in my life.

I looked around and saw one lone cherry tree with no limbs on it about 30 yards to my right, but my feet wouldn’t work. I knew I couldn’t stay where I was, but I couldn’t go anywhere else. Old Ripper just kept on coming. I finally threw that gun down and began to run. Then I saw Old Ripper, now 20 yards away, running on two crippled front legs. I knew then that I had a chance to outrun him, but just as that idea went through my mind, the big boar fell and rolled to a stop about 10 yards away from me. He never moved, he never grunted and he never made another sound.

There was a slight breeze coming from that dead boar to me. Old Ripper’s odor was the strongest, rankest smell I ever have smelled. It was awful. I waited awhile to make sure Old Ripper was dead. Then I looked to see where my bullets had hit. The first had entered the shoulder. The second went through the hog’s loin and had gone into his stomach. Two other shots had hit his fore shoulders and entered the chest cavity. One bullet just flat-out missed.

Looking at Old Ripper, I was kind of sad that he was gone. Even if he was a renegade, he was a magnificent animal. There had never been a boar like him before that I ever heard tell of, and there never was another.

Mrs. Ella T.’s son James and her husband Ressie helped me load Old Ripper onto the pickup truck. We took the boar to Mr. Smoke Roger’s platform scales at Fayetteville, Georgia. The boar tipped the scales at 438 pounds. We struggled to reload the boar and then drove back to Bainbridge. Dr. Cooper, the veterinarian at that time, examined him. Below Ripper’s inch-thick hide was a sheath of gristle that extended from his huge shoulders to the middle of his back. This sheath had been Old Ripper’s armor and had turned the shotgun pellets and rifle bullets over the years. Dr. Cooper said the boar was between 8 and 10 years old and was probably a throwback to some of the European wild boars let loose in this country years before.

Read Next: I’ve Been Charged by Bears and Moose. Wild Hogs Are Much, Much Worse

When my daddy saw that the boar filled up the bed of that pickup truck, he could hardly believe his eyes. He had wanted to be the one who killed Old Ripper, but since he didn’t, he was glad it was me.

“That ol’ hog has cost farmers in this area thousands of dollars and many good sows, as well as being responsible for a lot of little pigs that weren’t fit to sell,” my daddy said. “I’m glad he’s gone.”

Since then the old Fowltown Swamp where Old Ripper used to roam and where wild pigs lived and bred for hundreds of years has vanished. Old Ripper’s haunts are covered by Lake Seminole today, but I remember it like it was when that boar was less than 30 yards away on a dead run bringing hurt to me, and I heard the sound of the hammer on my .30/30 falling on an empty chamber.

#8336. 🥾 More Than a Trail, More Than Miles 🌄✨

Waking up to my watch alarm at 5:45 a.m., I grabbed a cup of coffee, then disappeared back into my dark room to write.

With laundry in the machine, I sat down with Nobody at the table. Another amazing meal: eggs and oat pancakes, fresh mango, and orange juice.

After eating a hot-out-of-the-oven brownie, I took one last foot bath.

Backpack packed, my tummy started rumbling.

I grabbed a few more brownies to eat on the road.

Almost to Walker Pass Campground, we passed a roadside burn from the night before. The sight of the burnt Joshua trees was devastating.

Arriving at Walker Pass, my stomach was still churning. After making two trips to the pit toilet, I swallowed an Imodium. I knew I could always turn around if I didn’t start feeling better.

As the sun began to dip toward the horizon, the trail leveled out. I set up my tent in the wind, wondering whether I should eat my leftover Pad Thai. I took half an Imodium, then ate my cold dinner.

Happy to be back in the wilderness, I fell asleep in my tent under the stars.

Pushing snooze on my 4 a.m. alarm, I fell back asleep, then repeated the process. I boiled water for oatmeal and coffee.

I took one more Imodium, then began my trek north at 7:20 a.m.

I thought about everything I was grateful for, especially being able to hike this trail. I was grateful to try those new tent stakes. I was also relieved that the fire near the trailhead had been extinguished, knowing how it could have affected the PCT.

Meeting Wings and Nobody was another thing I was grateful for.

Up, up went the trail. The sandy terrain gave way to the slate of the Sierras. The agave and blooming prickly pear disappeared, replaced with purple and red flowers.

Cresting a saddle, I pulled out my phone. Joshua Springs was three miles downhill. With my bottles empty, I crossed a small flowing stream, remembering Joshua Springs fondly from my 2022 hike. I planned a long lunch at the spring.

At a trail junction, I took a left and began my quarter-mile downhill hike. When I reached the piped water trough, I quickly realized that I could not expect this hike to be the same as my 2022 Sierra hike.

Hogs had come through and torn up the dirt. Since water was flowing along the trail above, hikers hadn’t needed to make the extra trip down to the spring.

Using my groundcloth to flatten the dirt, I sat down and took my shoes off while I filtered water. Mosquitoes and tiny gnats quickly became a nuisance while making a cheese, mayo, and barbecue chip burrito.

I preferred avoiding the midday heat, especially when I had access to shade and water. The conditions at the spring made it difficult to enjoy a restful break. Once my water was filtered, I hiked back up into the heat of the day.

A few miles later, I was sitting in the shade when I heard voices. Expecting to see hikers coming down the trail, I was surprised when two people popped out of the shrubs. Vic from PCTA and Andrea from the ACE crew were out for trail maintenance. We stopped to talk for a few minutes before I continued my hike.

At Spanish Needle Creek, I stopped to make dinner and filter water. I considered camping near the trail crew, but I still had a few miles left in me. I wanted to get a jump on the 11-plus-mile water carry.

As I hiked up a four-mile climb with 1,600 feet of elevation gain, I pulled out my headlamp. Eventually, I reached the Lamont Peak spur trail. I found a flat, rocky spot tucked away from the wind.

Setting up a freestanding tent in a rocky, windy location could be difficult for a beginner. I had always backpacked with freestanding tents and was proud of moments like this.

First, I wrapped the corner guyline around a small rock. Then I placed a larger rock on top of the guyline to keep the smaller rock from moving. I repeated this process on all the corners and then the doors. No stakes, my tent stayed up all night.

With no moon, the Milky Way was visible behind the bright stars.

Turning off my alarm, I fell back to sleep until the birds started singing.

While cold-soaking oatmeal in a bag, I took down my tent and talked with the couple I had camped near.

I crossed an unmarked water source, where I stopped to collect water and eat my oatmeal.

I passed near the jagged Sawtooth Peak, then switch-backed downhill. In the distance, I could see Chimney Mountain.

When I reached the wide-flowing Chimney Creek, I filtered water and grabbed a snack. After applying sunscreen, I was about to leave when I heard voices. I was surprised to see Joker, NBC, and All-Star behind me.

Mosby wasn’t feeling well and needed to get off trail. The five of us walked to Chimney Creek Campground, where we set our gear on a picnic table with a view of the gravel road.

When a vehicle approached, we flagged down the truck. Dulce and Chuck were going fishing and driving through Kennedy Meadows South.

With our backpacks in the bed of the truck, we all squeezed into the cab. We stopped at Grumpy Bear’s for a picture.

After being dropped off at the General Store, I saw a few hikers I knew: Sherpa, 8 Mile (previously Big Pharma), and Rooster.

After hearing about trail magic at the campground, I hitched one more time.

Hotdog and the Hike Beyond the Hills group had tacos for trail magic. TA Sprinter plucked at his guitar. Mary from 2 Foot stopped to visit for a while. Worms grabbed a bite on his hike north. Later, Snake Charmer, aka Mama Bear, made beef ramen with mushrooms and bok choy.

The evening was filled with good food and good company.

Borrowing trekking poles, I left my tent set up at Kennedy Meadows Campground. My bag was packed with the bare necessities and bulked out with my quilt.

Meeting up with Joker, Hotdog kindly drove the two of us back to Chimney Creek.

Sunshine (WA) was at Chimney Creek Campground, and we talked briefly. She was excited to be finishing her final PCT section!

Joker and I started our NOBO hike at 6 a.m.

As I passed a log swarming with black California carpenter bees, I noticed monarch butterflies everywhere.

Crossing over a stream, I met Marmot, Brave (Czech Republic), and Shake Head (Israel).

In the distance, I could see snow-covered, white-stone mountains dotted with pine trees.

Passing Mile 700, we stopped for a picture.

We talked with Michael, a day hiker and bird watcher.

When we reached the road, we walked to the General Store. There, Joker and I caught a ride back to the campground for more trail magic: grilled hot dogs.

That night, I met Cool Turkey, Honeyman, and Oliver.

That morning, I was able to sleep in and spend some time on my blog.

The girls—CeeCee, Vicki, and Rochelle—packed up camp and left.

We gave trail magic to Meta, a hiker attempting the Calendar Triple.

At Grumpy Bear’s, I retrieved my packages and unhappily paid to pick them up. After signing the logbook, I left.

Across the street, I picked up my PCT 2026 bandana and bought a HYOH sticker.

Back at the General Store for a shower and laundry, I purchased a green Alpha hoodie from 2 Foot Adventures.

I hung out with other hikers: Hellmann, Cactus, DQ, BangBang, Google, Rooster, Power Finger, Spice, Socks, and Bonus.

Back at the campground, I hung my clothes on a line to dry.

The wind blew a fine layer of sand inside my tent. My recently cleaned backpack had sand in the zippers, and I cleaned the sand out of my tent.

Seeing a shooting star was the cherry on top of my evening.

I was up way too early for a non-hiking day. At 4:30 a.m., it was a cold, gusty morning. Happy to have my new Alpha hoodie, I blogged and sipped coffee in the comfort of my tent.

Building a small fire for warmth, and the neighbor’s dog stopped over for a visit.

Around 8 a.m., the hikers started arriving for pancake trail magic on their way into the Sierras: BangBang, DQ, Joker, NBC, All-Star, Hellmann, Cactus, Brave, Rado, and Caroline.

After running out of pancakes, we made hot dogs. Google and more hikers continued arriving until all the food was gone.

Oyster came up needing a ride into town. She thought her filter was compromised.  Still a little while before we left, we asked the neighbor with the dog if he could give Oyster a ride.

At the General Store, I saw Fairy, and met a female hiker names Pickles.

Finally meeting back  up with Marble we talked about possibly going rafting down the Killer Kern. Excited for a possible side trip, I decided to hang out in KMS for a few more nights.

The afternoon was spent sorting my resupply into my bear can. Later, at the restaurant window, I ordered a cheeseburger with guacamole and a basket with half jalapeño poppers and half french fries.

Front Porch was having issues with his tent zipper. Fairy helped him fix it. I gave him my solar panel.

I spent the remainder of the evening painting my nails and watching YouTube.

I enjoyed coffee and pancakes with Front Porch, Marble, Pickles, and Electrolyte (MS).

With my resupply running low, I was grateful when hikers who were getting off trail offered to share their food. The extra meals and bars were much appreciated.

I back-flushed my filter and talked with Front Porch.

Hungry, I dug through the hiker box and threw together tomato soup with refried beans and ramen noodles. I added the chicken packet for flavor. It was really good for a hiker box meal.

That night, I met a lot of new hikers, including more women. It was nice to see how many women were on the trail this year.

As I crawled into my tent, the zipper started to act up, and it took me a while to get all the teeth to catch.

I am grateful for my ability to backpack.

I am grateful for humanity and the compassion people show one another.

I am grateful for the hiking community. There are some amazing people out there who help you along your journey. Their kindness is heartwarming.

I am proud to be a part of this community.

I am grateful for waking up on the trail each morning.
