#8281. Two Hikers Were Killed by a Sow Grizzly With Cubs In ‘Very Rare’ Predatory Attack

Published Nov 11, 2026 5:31 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack. A sow with three cubs killed two hikers, a mother-daughter pair who had been missing since November 1. DNA tests confirm the women were killed by the bears.

“It’s surreal. It doesn’t seem real,” Josh Balcarras, a family member, told CBC News. “The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them. That turns into a day, and then a night. Then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing.”

The remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2. The remains of her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed, were found November 3. The two were not far from a trail  in the steep and heavily-wooded Snooka Trail System. Both were buried in caches, something bears often do to hide their food from other animals. Investigators consider the attack to be motivated by predation.

“This attack involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Jeff Tyre, British Columbia Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) inspector said in a recorded statement issued November 10. “That is to say, we don’t know how it started but we know how it ended. Out of respect for the family, I’m going to decline to answer what predatory behavior looks like specifically in this case.”

The mother grizzly bear was in her late teens. Her three cubs were born this year. BCCOS announced November 10 that all four were captured and euthanized for their predatory behavior. A week after finding the remains of the second woman, the case is considered closed and trapping equipment has been removed. Nuxalk Nation cultural leaders will decide how the bear remains will be used.

“They all had to be destroyed because bears that are involved in attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre said. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

This most recent attack happened nearly a year after a grizzly attacked a group of tribal school children who were having lunch in the same region last November. In that case covered by OL, three students and one adult were hospitalized after a grizzly raided their picnic.

Despite the two high-profile incidents, investigators say grizzly bear attacks are not increasing near Bella Coola. They also cross-checked DNA from bears involved in both cases. None of the grizzlies euthanized this year were involved in the group attack last year. That bear was never located.

The tribe renewed its safety protocol during this year’s investigation. It has since lifted curfew but continues nightly patrols and offers escorts to take kids to school.

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” stated Samuel Schooner, Nuxalk Nation elected chief. “Our focus continues to be on taking care of our community members.”

Bella Coola is in the coastal region of British Columbia. Coastal bears and interior bears are genetically the same grizzly species, but their size and diet are different. Coastal bears have access to salmon, a nutrient-rich food source.

“Individual bears with increased access to salmon tend to be larger, have bigger litters, have lower stress hormone levels, and exist at higher densities at a population level,” reads an October 2025 study by Lauren Henson and Kris Christensen published in the scientific journal G3: Genes, Genomes and Genetics. “Interior grizzlies [have] smaller body mass and skull size than coastal individuals.”

Read Next: These Alaskans Stopped a Charging Grizzly at 5 Yards with Their 10mm Pistols

BC’s combined coastal and interior grizzly bear population has increased from 6,600 in the 1970s to 15,000 in 2018. In 2017, BC implemented a controversial grizzly bear hunting ban. Those in favor of the ban believe that a lack of grizzly hunting does not lead to more human fatalities, but organizations opposing the ban refer to recent attacks as reason to re-open the hunt.

“We have to do something,” Jesse Zeman, B.C. Wildlife Federation executive director told CBC News. “What we’re currently doing is very clearly not working.”

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#8280. Expert Tips for Scouting, Scattering, and Tagging Fall Turkeys

Fall turkey hunting requires matching your strategy to the specific flock type you're pursuing. Adult gobblers, hen-poult family groups, and second-year jakes all behave and vocalize differently. The spring yelp that pulled in a gobbler won't work in October. Identify the birds first, then dial in your calls and approach accordingly.

Turkeys typically only receive passing mentions when folks discuss their favorite fall pursuits. And with spring being a distant memory and other seasons in full swing, that’s understandable. And unfortunate. Fall turkeys offer a sporting experience unlike any other outdoors adventure. And with more than 40 states offering autumn turkey seasons—some of which open in September and others that run deep into winter—opportunities abound.

But the fall game plays out somewhat differently than the familiar spring ritual. Here’s a quick look at the types of turkeys you’ll likely encounter in the autumn woods and some tips on how to bring one home.

Many hunters kill fall turkeys incidentally while pursuing deer or small game, sometimes encountering flocks at harvested crop fields or mast-rich wooded areas. There’s nothing wrong with that, but true students of the autumn game dig far deeper into turkey behavior and learn to interact with each type of fall bird.

During fall, turkeys are in different modes than in spring, as they’re no longer concerned with breeding. Food and the struggle for survival dominate their existence. They typically fall into several distinct flock types: adult gobblers, hens without poults, and hens with broods of poults. Several subcategories also exist: Male birds in their second autumn—those that were jakes the previous spring—group together. These are sometimes called jake-and-a-halfs. Also, hen-poult groups often combine into larger family flocks, called crèches. The various groups sometimes intermingle, especially at prime feeding areas or large common roost sites. Often, however, you’ll encounter them separately.

As with spring, calling can be critical in autumn for finding turkeys and getting them close. However, turkeys—especially hens and poults—can be much more vocal in fall, and their lexicon expands to include sounds many spring hunters don’t hear much. Roost sites that attract family flocks can sound like a din of turkey chatter at dawn. Young turkeys often utter kee-kees (a series of three to four ascending whistles) and kee-kee runs, which are whistling series followed by a crude yelp or two. The vocalizations might sound slightly different depending on whether it’s uttered by a jake or jenny. Brood hens use long, pleading strings of assembly yelps to gather their offspring after being separated. Gobblers are typically less vocal in fall, communicating via slow, raspy gobbler yelps and popping clucks. Still, it’s not uncommon to hear them gobble at times.

Because the various types of turkeys act and vocalize differently in fall, general hunting approaches can fall flat. For example, the straightforward hen yelps that made a gobbler respond in April will likely be met with indifference from male turkeys in October. To boost your chances, you must know the kind of bird you’re hunting and then fine-tune your strategy.

Generally, fall hunts fall under two broad categories: 1) Hunters who call in an attempt to make turkeys come to them. 2) Hunters, or specially trained turkey dogs, who scatter groups of turkeys, then set up and try to call the birds back. Knowing the type of turkey you’re after is especially critical during scatter scenarios.

“You need to be the turkey that calls to you,” said Marlin Watkins, a noted Ohio call maker and expert fall turkey hunter. “A young gobbler is not coming to hen sounds. You need to be that bird, whether it’s a jenny hen, young gobbler, or adult hen. And if you produce those sounds, you will be far more successful.”

When his dogs scatter a flock, Watkins immediately tries to determine the group’s composition—hens, gobblers, or a family flock—as that will dictate his calling approach. “If I’ve scattered turkeys, I start with jenny hen kees and kee-kee runs, provided it’s a family flock,” he said. “As soon as first bird answers, I mimic that bird. A young gobbler is not coming to a jenny hen normally, so if a young gobbler kees and gobbler yelps, that’s what I do, even to the point of going note for note. As the bird approaches, I soften the calling, but I do not quit, or they will walk away. They can hear other birds calling that I can’t.”

Depending on the flock type, reassembling turkeys might present a shot opportunity within 20 or 30 minutes. However, adult hens and toms often take longer to get back together, so Watkins uses a different approach after flushing gangs of gobblers or jake-and-a-halfs. “We usually wait 30 minutes or more and start with gobbler yelping and clucking,” he said. “If we get no response in an hour or more, we will mix in gobbling. We start slow, only making a call or two every 10 or more minutes. After no response for that hour or more, we get a little more aggressive.”

That patient yet observant mindset can pay off, as it’s often unclear how birds will react. “I’ve broken gobblers one day and sat three hours, heard one cluck and then shot him,” Watkins said. “The very next day, I’ve broken a different flock, and they started gobbling in an hour and gobbled nonstop until we killed one. You just never know what they will do.”

When hunting alone, or in situations when you can’t scatter turkey flocks, calling strategies become more opportunistic. Brett Ladeau, a Vermont hunter and contest caller, often starts fall quests with a basic tactic. “I typically approach a fall hunt by finding roost sites and try to pattern either a family flock or mixed flock,” he said. “To locate birds, I scout much like I do in spring. I like to be close to birds while they are still on the roost, so finding roost areas is an important tactic I use to find fall birds. I scout for roosting areas and mark them on my mapping app for future hunts. If possible, I also like to watch or hear birds fly to the roost in the evening so I know where they will be in the morning.”

If a roost hunt doesn’t pan out, Ladeau tries to locate turkeys via calling, often taking a mobile approach. “I use my spring technique of riding from spot to spot where I know there are birds, and once I find a few spots that hold birds, I will cold-call at a few well-known turkey haunts,” he said.

And as with hunting scattered groups, Ladeau tries to match his calling to the vocalizations of responsive birds. “If I’m hunting a family group or mixed group, I will use the kee-kee a lot, along with assembly yelps and other calls,” he said. “If I’m hunting a mixed flock or a group of male birds, I will gobble- and jake-yelp to try to entice them into range. My setup is to try to get as close to the birds as possible and then start my calling sequence. If I’m close to a roost, I might not call much, especially if I know their routine, but if not, I call pretty aggressively.”

Get to know the flocks of autumn this year, and fine-tune your calling to bring them into shooting range. Ducks and big bucks can wait a bit as you enjoy the sights and sounds of the fall turkey woods.

#8279. The Best Tech Gifts for Gear Nerds Who Actually Go Outside

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

There’s plenty of outdoor tech that nobody really needs. But the gear on this list earns its keep in battery life, from a watch built for massive days in the mountains to a cooler that eliminates floating cheese and a torch that quickly turns kindling into a substantial fire. We dug through the specs to find gadgets that actually make time outside easier, safer, and more fun.

I enjoy the quiet romance of coaxing damp wood into a fire with tiny pieces of kindling, but I appreciate a gigantic blast of flame even more. Pump up the heat with Snow Peak’s Folding Torch, which threads onto an isobutane canister and produces a concentrated flame that lights charcoal and stubborn firewood quickly. The stainless steel, aluminum, brass, and natural-wood handle make the 10.1-ounce tool incredibly handsome, and the head folds for storage. Some may call this cheating, but it can be a lifesaver on a cold, rainy night, and is also very fun to use.

Thanks to its low weight and everyday utility, the Nitecore NB10000 Gen 2 Power Bank is a smart item to bring backpacking rather than a luxury. Its carbon-fiber shell helps keep 10,000mAh of battery capacity below six ounces—enough for roughly two smartphone charges depending on the phone and conditions. That’s a lot of navigational, photographic, and emergency juice for very little pack weight.

The NESTOUT Starter Pack Bundle is a capable charger that doubles as a genuinely solid little camp light whenever you need one. It combines a 5,000mAh, 4.9-ounce power bank with a modular lantern and mini tripod. The light adjusts from 10 to 300 lumens and can run up to 24 hours at its lowest brightness, while the IP67-rated battery is resistant to dust and water.

Changing disposable coin batteries in a device you wear while measuring state-of-the-art fitness data is ridiculously antiquated and annoying. Wahoo’s TRACKR Heart Rate Monitor is rechargeable, with more than 100 hours of active battery life between charges. The 1.4-ounce unit broadcasts over ANT+ and can connect to three Bluetooth devices simultaneously, while an IPX7 rating protects it from sweat and rain.

Binoculars make every outdoor trip more interesting, but an oversized pair is a hassle to carry. Nocs’s Field Issue 8×42 combines full-size optics with a unique, durable, and fun design, in a compact body that weighs just 1.3 pounds. The nitrogen-filled body is IPX7 waterproof, the fully multicoated lenses and BaK4 roof prisms sharpen the image, and a 394-foot field of view at 1,000 yards makes moving animals easier to track. Once you’ve used them, you won’t forget them at home.

There’s a lot of tech out there that can help you track your health and fitness, but none are as comprehensive as the Hume Pod Smart Body Composition Scale. Tracking 45 different metrics, the scale can help you monitor muscle gain, fat loss, body water, and even your metabolic age. 98% accurate against a DEXA scan, the 8-frequency sensors and dual-point contact scan your whole body, not just your lower half like other standard smart scales, giving you the most holistic look at your body’s metrics. Multiple users can track on a single pod, and the free app makes it easy to evaluate your progress and sync with your Apple Health, Fitbit, or Garmin. Paid for by Hume Health

Running exhausted in the dark is terrifying, which makes the Distance 1500 a high-tech gem. Black Diamond pulled out all the technology stops to build this headlamp for ultrarunners moving fast at night through technical terrain. The 1,500 lumen output is impressive in itself, but other run-specific features make it even more so, including the maximum beam distance of 117 meters and a low-profile Comfort Cradle designed to reduce bouncing.

Few things make me irrationally angry faster than being awakened by a stranger slamming a hotel door at 2 in the morning. Ozlo’s Sleepbuds 2 are tiny, 1.6-gram earbuds specifically shaped to be worn sleeping—side sleepers included!—and deliver up to 14 hours of battery life. They can stream audio or play noise-masking sounds designed to cover disruptions like traffic and snoring, making them an ideal gift for frequent travelers and light sleepers.

The DB2 Bluetooth speaker is built inside a genuine Pelican case and carries an IP67 waterproof rating when sealed. Two three-inch speakers crank to around 94 decibels (i.e., loud enough to rock a four-net beach volleyball party), battery life stretches to roughly 40 hours at full volume, and the interior compartment doubles as dry storage. At 5.44 pounds, it’s hefty, but that’s a trade I’m happy to make for a speaker that doesn’t need babysitting on rafting trips and wet beach days.

Suunto’s Vertical 2 is way more watch than a casual runner needs, which is exactly why it’s the perfect gift for a type A athlete. A bananas feature set includes 65 hours of multiband GPS tracking, 32GB of offline map storage, and a bright 1.5-inch AMOLED screen that makes those maps usable in the middle of big runs. We’ve also found the LED flashlight incredibly capable: handy around camp and a lifesaver when runs take longer than expected.

Goal Zero’s Yeti 700 turns any campsite into a usable office if someone wants to run lights and laptops at camp. Back at home, it doubles as a capable backup during a power outage. At 20.3 pounds, it is a beast in size and function, with enough battery capacity to run a 100-watt device for roughly six hours and a construction designed to withstand thousands of recharges. Its 600-watt output is enough to handle laptops, lights, and plenty of smaller camp electronics, and it only takes two hours to charge from a wall socket at home.

The problem with drones is that getting great drone footage usually requires someone to stop messing around, step away from the action, and seriously pilot the thing. HoverAir’s X1 uses automated subject tracking and hands-free filming tools so solo athletes can get dynamic footage without recruiting an unpaid film crew every weekend. It’s the perfect gift for the person who wants to stay present on their adventures while also capturing footage of what they did.

Once you use an electric cooler for a long car trip, returning to bags of ice and floating cheese feels barbaric. Dometic’s 75-liter CFX5 has two independently controlled compartments, so one side can freeze while the other refrigerates. Vacuum-insulated panels improve thermal efficiency, while the VMSO 3.5 compressor can pull temperatures down to minus 7 degrees Fahrenheit. It runs from AC or vehicle power and works with compatible battery and solar systems. The 113-can capacity makes this more like a mobile kitchen appliance than a traditional cooler.

#8278. The Best Ski Gear for Powder Days and Storm Chasing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Chasing powder this winter? These tester-favorite skis, boots, shell, goggles and avalanche gear keep you dry, safe and skiing deep all storm cycle long. (Photo: Ray J Gadd)

Storm chasing is what most skiers dream about. One minute you’re scrolling the forecast from your desk, the next you’re cramming gear into a bag and packing up the car or hopping on a flight to score some freshies. It’s how we’d all love to spend our winters, sniffing out the best forecasts and bouncing between deep days around the country. With a strong, possibly historic El Niño predicted for this winter, there’s no telling exactly where the storm track will decide to unload. Nailing a good storm cycle takes patience, a little planning and a willingness to drop everything and go when the conditions allow. That, and the right gear to stay dry and comfortable all day long on the mountain—nothing kills a day faster than soaking wet mittens or fogged-up goggles.

Here’s the ski setup, storm-ready layers, and safety essentials our testers have long counted on for traveling far and wide to chase the biggest storms—plus a rolling bag to get it all there. Because the more dialed your gear is, the more time you can spend hunting for powder stashes. Pair these gear recs with SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide, the best tool for getting familiar with resorts across North America. That way, you’ll have a shortlist of options ready when the snow starts flying, wherever El Niño sends it.

If you have to choose just one ski for a powder-hunting mission, the Salomon S/Lab QST X is our top choice. With a 116-millimeter waist and freeride rocker profile, these sticks were made to float through champagne powder as well as dense, surfy snow, with a caruba and poplar wood core that’s light and lively. Flax and carbon fibers plus cork in the tip and tail keep things smooth and stable—a ski that can stand up to hard-charging freeriders but remains accessible for intermediates. Its midweight design—2,000 grams per ski at the 184 centimeter length—allows skiers to ride all day inbounds or mount up a hybrid binding for dropping out of bounds.

Even on a resort trip, it’s nice to keep your options open. If your plan is to primarily ski inbounds with a few short tours, the Salomon S/Lab Shift 2 10 MN Bindings are your ticket to ultimate flexibility. Salomon redesigned the Shift bindings this year, beefing up the construction in the heel and toe to help prevent pre-release and boost durability. On snow, most skiers won’t notice a big sacrifice compared with a traditional alpine binding, and you get the added benefit of a tour-capable binding perfect for a quick tour when the terrain across the valley beckons.

No one wants to tote around a second pair of boots on a ski trip. Tecnica’s new Zero G Decoy Pro boots are powerful hybrids, an ideal one-boot solution for deep trips. The Decoy delivers solid inbounds performance thanks to a stiff 130 flex, and the walk-mode lever is easy to flip with gloves on, making it simple to power up a bootpack or skintrack—or just cruise around the base area without killing your feet.

For deep days inbounds and in the backcountry, the 3-layer PowSlayer jacket and pants—available in men’s and women’s—provide ample protection without weighing you down. Powder days are full of temperature swings, and the PowSlayer kit uses a Gore-Tex ePE membrane, which repels moisture while regulating your body temp as you transition from frigid summits to top-to-bottom runs. The jacket sports a cinchable storm hood for blustery lift rides, and the pants feature a sewn-in pocket for stowing a transceiver securely.

Visibility is often limited on the deep days we dream of, and high-performance goggles become more crucial than ever. Smith’s 4D MAG ChromaPop Goggles with an extra lens offer a large field of view and the option of a photochromic lens, which is ideal on days when the light flows in and out as a storm moves through. Lens swapping is easy with these—a magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out during a quick gondola ride.

For deep days when it feels like fresh snow is sneaking into every little crevice, cinch up Black Diamond’s Mercury Mittens and consider the problem solved. A toasty fleece-lined gauntlet design delivers ample coverage while you explore the white room, and a waterproof BD.dry insert keeps your hands dry all day long. Synthetic insulation is low-profile, and the 4-way stretch shell provides a comfortable fit that lets you grip your poles securely.

An extra neckwarmer is crucial for storm skiing, and having a dry one on hand to swap in midday can easily add a few extra hours to your day. Skida’s Alpine Neckwarmer provides cozy relief from frigid wind, with a stretchy polyester shell that sheds moisture, and a fleece lining that’s like a hug for your face. The Alpine Neckwarmer is ideal for those uber-chilly powder days, while a lighter option such as the Snow Tour can be great for warmer PNW storms.

Low-profile yet spacious, the Dakine Heli Pro 20L Backpack is compact enough to ride chairs all day, with enough space for shorter ski tours and out-of-bounds laps. There’s a dedicated safety pocket to stash your shovel and probe, as well as a fleece-lined goggle pocket to protect your goggles while you hike, or keep an extra lens on hand for fogging emergencies. There are both diagonal and A-frame carry options, so it’s easy to stow your skis for quick bootpacks.

A beacon is a necessity for skiing out of bounds, and it’s never a bad idea to switch yours on for deep days at the resort as well. The industry-leading beacon for professionals and advanced skiers alike, Mammut’s Barryvox S2 Beacon features all the bells and whistles you’d want out of a pro-level device: Group Check modes, an advanced flagging feature and a 70-meter range. #8275. I Retraced Jennifer Nelson’s Final Steps to an Abandoned Colorado Mine

An abandoned mining feature on Red Mountain Pass near Ouray, Colorado (Photo: Roger Lord Photography)

The mine shaft is still open and breathing, an eight-foot-wide hole in the Earth with no flowers set beside it, no memorial, only blocked now by a black mesh fence and a red sign inscribed with four words: Stay Out Stay Alive. It is set back under the shadows of towering spruce and fir, 90 feet up a moss-covered hill off an old mining road in the San Juan Mountains, where I have come on a late summer afternoon to retrace the last steps of Jennifer Nelson.

I hold onto a lodgepole and creep over the weathered fence, just far enough to see the mine’s exposed flat rock walls disappear into the ground, enough to see that if anyone were to fall in, they wouldn’t be able to climb out. The canopy of trees drowns out all light, but down the slope, the sun bathes grey rock on the trail.

It is easy to understand why Jennifer loved this area, why she had come here on October 20, 2025, the last day of her life. I had made the short drive from her home in Ridgway, Colorado, and up the Million Dollar Highway over Red Mountain Pass, weaving my way through the San Juans until I reached a narrow dirt lip on an old mining road. I parked next to a grizzled hiker who looked exhausted. “Howdy,” he had said, pulling off his boots on the bumper of a 4Runner. I waved and slipped around a green gate that keeps vehicles off the trail.

My boots crunched the gravel, and there was no other sound, except for the distant hum of an electrical substation nearby. The trail was framed with views of the Red Mountains, and as I glanced over my shoulder back at the highway, I saw the rooftops of the historic Idarado Houses, built more than 100 years before for miners and their families in the abandoned ghost town of Eureka, Colorado.

The trail, too, was littered with rusted relics from mining camps: a half-buried oil can with chipped teal paint, an oxidized metal tool tray and, tucked away in a meadow, a buck-and-pole corral, once used to shepherd mules and horses that hauled silver and copper down the mountain. I had been told the mine was hidden in the trees, only a quarter-mile up, and I realized I had walked right past it. I carefully backtracked, looking for any sign, and when I finally spotted the top of the black fence in the timber up above the trail, my heart jumped into my throat. I thought of Jennifer.

At 54, she had already collected a lifetime of adventures in the backcountry, and when she arrived here for another hike on a Monday afternoon in October, she found a reprieve from life as the owner of a pet-sitting business and member of Ridgway’s planning commission. She needed these walks, both for peace of mind and for her ailing back, which always felt better after she finished a trek in the woods.

The mountain had spotty cell service, and she could walk uninterrupted while her dogs trotted alongside her. Earlier that day, over lunch, she had told her husband, Jeff Rivera, that she was headed up to the trail. She’d take Mia, their border collie mix, and another dog she was looking after for a friend.

“Be careful,” he told her, but he otherwise wasn’t worried: she knew the trail like the back of her hand, and Jeff thought it was just another day in the life Jennifer had dreamed of living when she moved from Denver to the San Juans a decade earlier. He went back to work that afternoon, but by the time he returned home again that evening, Jeff thought she would already be home, too. He texted Jennifer: “What do you want for dinner?”

There was no answer, and by 5:30 P.M., he grew worried. It was starting to get dark. Jeff hopped into his Ford F-150 and sped up the Million Dollar Highway, hoping to see Jennifer pass him on her way down, but when he arrived at the trailhead, he found her Toyota Tundra empty.

He squeezed past the green gate and ran up the mountain. The temperature had dropped, and he could see his breath as he screamed her name. Jeff had seen a lot as a volunteer firefighter in Ridgway, but nothing could prepare him for this. Without a cell signal, he ran back down the trail to call 911, to tell the police that his wife was missing.

Grant Kleeves was at home eating dinner when his pager went off. He had been a member of the Ouray Mountain Rescue team for a decade, serving now as a lieutenant, and his evenings were often interrupted with calls to search for missing people in the backcountry. This message was no different: a woman had failed to return from a hike on Red Mountain Pass, so Kleeves met his team at the clubhouse to grab equipment before making the trek up the mountain.

The unit arrived with three trucks and an all-terrain vehicle in tow, cracking open the green gate to prowl the trail. A search team on foot canvassed hundreds of yards on the flanks of the trail, hoping to catch a glimpse of Jennifer through the beams of their flashlights. The trail snakes up the mountain for more than two miles, and there were obvious places to check, including a small pond and larger mines that often served as tourist attractions for hikers. None of those places turned up a clue. A drone was launched into the dark sky, and Kleeves hoped its thermal-detection capabilities could turn up a lead. But the temperatures had dropped to about 30 degrees that night, and the batteries were dying quickly.

Jeff raced back down the mountain to Ridgway in his Ford, and when he arrived back at his house, he grabbed a winter coat and some gloves before heading back up to the trail. He parked next to Jennifer’s truck and decided he wanted to let the rescue team do their jobs. It was dark and quiet, and he stared up at the trees, waiting, hoping Jennifer and the dogs might all of a sudden appear behind the people up on the mountain looking for them.

After nearly four hours of searching, Kleeves and his teammates backtracked toward the vehicles at the front of the trail to make a new plan, to launch a second tier of the search. It was in the wee hours of the morning now, and they’d need to get more people involved, Kleeves thought, to cast a wider net across the area. A 4Runner drove ahead of Kleeves, beaming light into the treeline. About a quarter-mile from the trailhead, Kleeves’s headlamp caught a glint of something near a berm. He craned his neck and shone light back toward the reflection and saw the green glow of a dog’s eyes. Kleeves believed the dog had popped its head up to look at the commotion of the rescue down on the trail. Kleeves whistled and caught the eyes of a second dog.

Kleeves and his team walked up the slope toward the animals. The team’s headlamps caught the dark shadow of a gash in the ground, and as they stepped closer, they recognized it as an unmarked mine shaft. Near the opening, a backpack and hat rested on the ground, and a lone trekking pole leaned against a fallen tree. The dogs stared silently at the volunteers as they stood at the edge of the mine. Kleeves shone his light into the hole, and about ten feet down from the surface, he could see a body floating in water, face down.

Below, toward the trailhead, Jeff was within earshot of radio chatter, so Kleeves didn’t want to be careless when his team radioed that they needed assistance on the hill. Even though this appeared to be a terrible accident, his team wanted to treat it like a crime scene and not touch anything. Soon more police and paramedic vehicles hauled up the highway. Jeff knew something terrible had happened, and eventually the county coroner walked over to his truck window. “They found her in a mine shaft, and she drowned,” he remembered the coroner telling him, but Jeff was in such disbelief that he thought maybe he didn’t hear the words right, that maybe it wasn’t actually Jennifer in that shaft.

Soon reality set in, and Jeff’s fire chief drove up to the trailhead to pull him away from the scene. Jeff gathered the dogs into the truck, and he could tell they were still shaken. He held Mia, the only witness to Jennifer’s final moments, and as the sun came up, he sat in his living room with the fire chief. Jeff began to talk to Jennifer.

“What the hell were you doing there?” he kept asking, and as the days passed, he replayed all of the scenarios in his head. Jennifer’s backpack was left to the side of the mine, but he didn’t know why she would have taken it off. Investigators noted that the dogs were not wet when they were found several hours later. Jeff wondered: did one of the animals fall in, prompting Jennifer to jump in after it? He knew a moose had been spotted in the area. Did it spook her when she was sitting at the edge and cause her to fall in?

Other details that didn’t add up rattled in his brain: the dog leashes were nowhere to be found at the scene. And he believes Jennifer had her phone in her hand after she had fallen into the water. Investigators found the phone on the west edge of the shaft; the ground around the phone had been obviously disturbed, as if Jennifer had desperately clung to the earth before falling in. There was also a two-foot branch, broken on both sides, found in the water alongside her body; up above, a log hanging over the edge of the mine had a middle section missing. It appeared to match the wood that was in the water. A Ouray County Sheriff’s Deputy who investigated the scene, Brady Suppeland, explained what he believed happened in his report on the incident:

“My initial instinct of what likely occurred was Jennifer likely had followed the dogs off trail up to that location for an unknown reason, and had fallen into the water unable to pull herself out,” Suppeland wrote. “It is possible the section of tree in the water broke while Jennifer was standing or holding onto it causing her to fall in, or it broke as she tried to use it to climb out. It appeared she had extensively tried climbing out where her phone was located as the dirt had been pulled from the hillside into the hole. There was some exposed tree roots in this area that would have given her something to grip to get her out of the water and onto the edge of the shaft, but not enough to pull herself all the way out. It appeared as she was attempting to manipulate her phone while hanging on the edge of the opening.”

Jennifer had tried texting Jeff during her last moments, but the messages didn’t go through.

“Hel,” she wrote at 5:36 P.M. A little more than an hour later, she tried sending her final plea.

They had just celebrated their six-year wedding anniversary. Jeff was a widower when they started dating; his first wife of 30 years, Dawn, had passed away from cancer in 2016, and in the years after, Jennifer had helped him begin to heal. Everyone seemed to gravitate toward her: she was warm and kind, with an inviting smile and a quiet, steady laugh. Jeff shared her love for the Denver Broncos, classic rock, and animals, and they both felt lucky to live on the edge of the San Juans, at nearly 7,000 feet, in Ridgway. They looked out their window every morning and marveled at 14,150-foot Mount Sneffels, and they went to work each day to make their small town better. Jeff worked for the city and the fire department, while Jennifer sat on the planning commission.

Nearly every weekend, Jennifer would nudge Jeff to take her to the mountains, always reminding him that, after being born and raised in Denver, she had moved to Ridgway to be closer to nature and there was no time to waste. They were always camping or hunting or looking for antler sheds, and sometimes they would disappear for days at a time. Just a few years earlier, a family member had reported them missing after they didn’t return from a camping trip for a couple days. They eventually emerged from the woods to find locals had been worried and looking for them; they laughed about it later, because they were simply enjoying themselves in the forest without cell service.

Now Jennifer wasn’t coming back. Officials told Jeff he could identify her body at the rescue team’s barn later that morning, but he couldn’t bring himself to do it. First, the team had to pull Jennifer out of the mine. The shaft’s walls were flat stone and wet. There was a tree overhanging the pit, so the team rigged up two rope systems: one for Kleeves to lower himself into the hole to get a rope around Jennifer, and one to act as a crane to lift her out.

Kleeves considered himself a serious climber. He climbed four or five days a week and had been doing it for 20 years. But he doubted even he could negotiate his way out of the shaft had he fallen in. “It was sobering, because usually I figure I can climb out of just about anything,” he says. “And dropping down into there was one of those where I was like, ‘That is…absolutely terrifying.’”

He had a hard enough time keeping his footing when his team lowered him into the hole. He swayed back and forth, his feet slipping off the shaft’s slick walls. He finally anchored himself to the slick surface. He wrapped a rope around Jennifer and tied it, and his team above, with a body bag waiting, lifted her into the air.

The shock of Jennifer’s death coursed its way across the state, to the Denver offices of Colorado’s Division of Reclamation, Mining, and Safety, where a core tenet was to protect the public from the dangers of abandoned mines. The director of the active and inactive mines reclamation program, Jeff Graves, had grown up drawn to the outdoors and to the history of mines, and for nearly two decades, he felt lucky to be able to marry his interests working for the state. But this was the worst part of the job, when someone was seriously injured or killed in a mine.

The state kept no official list of casualties, but the memories haunted him, including eight years before, when a 15-year-old had skipped class with some friends and rappelled into an abandoned clay mine in Jefferson County. The rope snapped, and the boy fell 60 feet to the bottom of the hole. He was trapped, with a broken leg. Rescue crews worked for three hours to pull him out while a news helicopter hovered overhead, and Graves watched it unfold on his television.

“In any instance when we’re not able to get out there before something like this happens, it’s difficult,” he says, and what made Jennifer’s death even more difficult was that there were thousands more of the kind of unmarked shafts that she had died in. Before Jennifer’s death, the state was unaware of the mine that she had plunged into; it had not been logged in the program’s inventory or targeted for closure, simply because nobody from the office knew it existed.

When Colorado launched the abandoned mine program in 1980, it estimated there were 23,000 mining sites that posed a physical hazard and needed to be addressed. Graves estimates that, across Colorado, between 40,000 and 50,000 sites still require some type of remediation for safety. “We don’t know where all of those are,” Graves tells me. “We have an idea, at least where in general sites are, based on where historic mining took place in Colorado, but specific locations of every single mine in Colorado?  We certainly don’t have that information, and it would be difficult, if not impossible, to collect that data. It’d be a monumental task to do that. So we just kind of chip away at that process in areas where we know there’s been historic mining.”

One of those areas is in the western part of Boulder County, where Graves invites me in August to tour an abandoned mine site. He steers his blue Ford Ranger onto an old gravel road. A teal Yeti bike is clipped to the back of the rig, and a softball-sized purple fluorite rock rolls along the floor of the cab. He parks near a mountainside once rollicking with mining camps.

Graves wears a few days of scruff, with a blue-collared shirt tucked into grey canvas pants. His logging boots crunch on pine needles as he hikes up the mountainside. His colleague, Rachael Nickless, an environmental specialist with the program, is among those who have joined us, and as we approach the mine, Graves ducks under a branch and imagines how prospectors might’ve picked this area, likely sticking dynamite in the ground to see what flew up.

“Think about what took place here,” he marvels, and soon we see the remnants of a towering ore bin structure, its timbered-planked walls still standing on rough-cut posts lodged into the slope. Derelict cables dangle from the top. A massive steel wheel-drum, once the cog to move thousands of pounds of minerals, sits idle. A fence has been erected around the structure, but through the boards, I can still see inside. There’s an opening that drops more than 100 feet into the ground. Around the corner, I notice a bright orange sign attached to the fence, with three skulls and a warning:

In the 46 years that the abandoned mine program has existed in Colorado, about 14,000 mines have been remediated. Graves has more than a dozen project managers spread out across the state, developing relationships with agents from the Bureau of Land Management and U.S. Forest Service and private landowners themselves; often, the team relies on a hodgepodge of information, using geological surveys, remote sensing tools, and old-fashioned tips from the public to find and assess abandoned sites.

A mine can be remediated in a variety of ways and can be as simple as backfilling a shaft with soil and rock that is near the surface of the opening. Polyurethane foam is often used to seal open holes; officials also use steel grating as fencing over horizontal and vertical mines, which keeps humans out but gives access to wildlife for habitat.

Erosion and vegetation can obscure openings from being discovered, but even sites that have been worked on can require maintenance years later. The mine Graves shows me was once pumped full of polyurethane that didn’t hold, and the week before, he and Nickless had traveled to the site and weighed the options to refill it or fence it off. He points up the mountain: in 2013, a 1,000-year rain event swept through the area, causing erosion at other sites that had been addressed. “These sites are always changing,” he says. “Fires, floods, they’re dynamic sites that evolve.”

The only thing he knew that wouldn’t change would be people’s curiosity—or sometimes, blindness—to these places, and not just in Colorado. The problem was felt in every corner of the country. “As many as half a million abandoned mines are believed to exist, and the location of many more is still unknown,” the Bureau of Land Management concedes on its website. “Usually, sites have no signage at all to warn people about their presence or their dangers.”

Jennifer’s death rattled officials with abandoned mine programs in states across the country, where tens of thousands of mines remain potential death traps for adventurers in the backcountry. Fatalities are rare, but serious accidents in recent years have provided a stark reminder of the sheer volume of unmarked mines and the hazards they can pose. In Pennsylvania in 2024, a 64-year-old grandmother died after falling 30 feet into a sinkhole connected to an abandoned coal mine. In California in 2023, three hikers had to be rescued after falling into a shaft; in 2019 in Arizona, a runner was injured and stranded after falling into a mine; in Utah, a self-described “adept rock-climber” had to be rescued in 2020 after rappelling into a shaft, and in 2024, a 62-year-old man planned to do the same—outfitting himself with a helmet, harness, and rope—but the edge of the mine gave way as he tried to climb in. He fell 50 feet into the mine and suffered traumatic brain injuries.

“We’ve closed about 7,000 mines, and there’s probably 10,000 remaining,” says Steve Fluke, who runs Utah’s abandoned mine program. Utah officials find between 200 and 300 mines per year, Fluke says, and while they’ve launched a campaign in schools to teach kids about the dangers of mines, there’s only so much they can do to protect the public from the hazards of these relics.

Many states are also strapped for resources and perpetually fighting for funding. Colorado’s abandoned mine program budget sits at about $13 million, Graves says, with only about $250,000 devoted to finding and closing hardrock mines; there’s historically been more money available for coal mining closure projects. “The area where Jennifer was found is a hardrock area. We’re pushing Congress to address more hard rock,” Graves tells me.

After he shows me the remains of the massive ore bin, he walks further up the mountain, carefully studying the ground and pointing out craters in the landscape that never quite became mines. “There are thousands of these across Colorado,” he tells me, as if we’re looking at some kind of monument of the Wild West. We both imagine settlers running around this forest, digging holes into the ground, some deeper than others, and then we think of all the other places across the West where folks were doing the same.

“What you see in the West, in terms of infrastructure, towns, everything’s a result of mining,” Graves says. “I mean, eventually, people would have ended up here. But probably not in a lot of these mountain communities, because it was hard to make a living here. You’re not gonna farm here. So the only way you made a living was to mine. And so that’s what drove expansion West, was that desire to find gold.”

Graves looks at an old can and guesses its age—maybe an artifact from the 1940s?—and the possible remnants of a teacup, which might suggest this was once a site where miners would bring their families.

We cross a creek near the highway to look at another mine across the water, a shaft exposed after the floods of 2013 swept through the timber and opened it up. The day he came to investigate, teenagers were walking out of it, leaving behind trash. Photos of the mine were posted on Facebook by enthusiasts and explorers. Graves and his team have sometimes discovered mines and shut them down by monitoring that activity, but often people who want to visit abandoned sites remain discreet.

“They kind of got onto us, and then made sure that in their group discussions, nobody tells people where the site is,” he tells me. “We had a way of tracking it and our efforts to kind of get in front of it ended up getting us shut out of it.”

He stares at the steel grate over the shaft opening and guesses some kind of metallic material, maybe gold or silver, was once mined here in the late 1800s. Mine closures could take months at a time, because officials conduct environmental studies and consider historic preservation of sites.

While we study the mine across the creek, Nickless stays by the truck down on the highway, where she notices another mine, a horizontal shaft in the side of a hill that was closed by their team at some point.

“There’s one over here too!” Nickless screams, her voice echoing across the creek and through the pines. Graves turns around and squints at the mine.

“Oh my God,” he says, as if he were looking at the shaft for the first time. “Who even knew? Like I said, they’re everywhere.”

In Ridgway, Jennifer’s death remains a mystery with enduring questions. Why had she traveled the 90 feet off the trail toward the shaft? How’d she fall in? And why hadn’t the mine been found earlier and closed off?

The town has roughly 1,000 residents but is brimming with character; it is known as a hub for local artists and a beacon of history. Built as a railroad town, it once connected the mining communities of Telluride and Ouray. The John Wayne film True Grit was shot in Ridgway, and Jennifer had known the owners of the True Grit Cafe on North Lena Street. She knew everyone, really; her pet-sitting business had more than two dozen loyal customers, and locals felt close to her because of how she took care of their dogs, cats, and horses.

Ridgway has always been resilient; locals sometimes refer to it as “The Town that Refused to Die.” Over the years, not only has it survived forest fires, the Great Depression, and the eventual loss of its once-booming railroad industry, but its citizens have also staved off plans to submerge the town under water with a proposed reservoir project in the 1970s. It would have to be resilient again: the town’s mayor, John Clark, had lived in Ridgway for 44 years but had rarely seen the town grapple with a tragedy as confounding as Jennifer’s death. “It’s just been a shocker,” he says.

On a Wednesday evening in August, Clark rides his bike to town hall, a simple one-story lodge with green carpet and landscape photographs of the mountains that surround Ridgway. He has a thick beard and dark-rimmed glasses. I’m the only attendee at the monthly planning commission meeting. John sits in the center, and to his left is Michelle Montague, the group’s acting chairperson.

The windows are open, and the laughter of kids playing in a nearby park creeps into the room. A few minutes before roll call begins, I introduce myself to everyone, and Montague waves and points to the chair next to her. “Jennifer sat right there,” she says. Everyone grows silent for a moment. Jennifer was proud of Ridgway and its celebrated history, which was inextricably linked with mining, and in her role on the planning commission, she was known to fiercely hold outside developers’ feet to the fire if she believed their projects would change the soul of her town.

The planning commission has carried on without her, and as the meeting begins, the commissioners discuss a bevy of topics, about the local summer concert series and farmers market, about targeted coding updates and historic development preferences. They pull out maps and talk about mixed-use projects, about vacant lots in town next to power facilities and sewer plants, and what might be built next door. “Ridgway’s pretty eclectic,” Montague tells the commissioners. “I don’t know exactly what this looks like, and I think that there have to be some parameters so that someone can design something and bring it in, because otherwise it’s not just wide open, like, ‘Do whatever you want.’”

The meeting wraps up and afterward, the commissioners mingle. Jennifer had told one of them in the fall of 2025 about how excited she was for the next part of her life, and a few days after she died, they held a moment of silence for her before their meeting. “It’s really strange,” Montague tells me after the meeting. “When you lose someone, they’re just like, gone. Just not here anymore. And I haven’t heard any follow- up on what happened with the mine, if they closed that off.”

I told her a few hours before I had hiked up to the mine and that it had not been covered but had a fence installed around its perimeter. Montague relays this to Clark as he packs his belongings and prepares to depart.

“There’s been no reclamation done on that mine that Jennifer fell in,” Montague says. “Like, that could happen again.”

“I’m sure it’s probably on someone’s list,” Clark says.

“I’m not going to be too psyched if I fall in there and think, ‘Oh, it was on someone’s list,’” she replies. “Maybe they should just put a cell phone in there so if you fall in, you can call for help.”

In September 2026, Glenn Boyd, the Ouray County coroner, released the results of Jennifer’s autopsy, announcing she had drowned and that her death was an accident. There was a frothy fluid in Jennifer’s airways and watery fluid with wood debris found in her stomach, and hypothermia was determined to have also contributed to her death. The shaft’s water was just 30 degrees. Jennifer had also suffered minor blunt force injuries: scratches, bruises, and focal subcutaneous hemorrhages of the head, neck, and extremities.

“Her cell phone data showed that Mrs. Nelson attempted to text her husband for help twice, but the messages were not delivered,” the report says.

Those unsent messages tore Jeff up. He had found photos from that day on Jennifer’s phone, taken of the dogs near the treeline on the trail, but the messages reminded him of how much she must have struggled in the water.

Only theories were left. In the days after the incident, the Colorado Bureau of Investigation had shown up at his house to ask him a host of questions, he says, including about Jennifer’s mouthguard found near the mine and a bluetooth speaker she had kept in her truck. He had told them everything he knew. The local newspaper, the Ouray Plaindealer, had reported in September that investigators had attempted to drain the shaft to look for more evidence, but gave up after pumping nine feet of water and seeing no bottom.

“They never told me anything about that,” Jeff says.

About two weeks before the autopsy was released, he did receive a call with an update on the mine: the shaft had been covered by a metal grate and permanently closed by the state.

Before I leave Ridgway, I meet Jeff at a local cafe, not far from where he shared a home with Jennifer. He’s been up since 3 A.M., fixing a leak in Ridgway’s water main. His clothes had been soaked, so he changed into a dry pair to eat lunch, much like he did on the last day he saw his wife. We sit in the sun at a table on the sidewalk, with a view of the mountains, and for the first time since knowing him, he lets out a laugh when he tells me of his first date with Jennifer. “It was on a weekend…I texted her, and she texted me back: ‘Well, I’m going hiking.’”

“I said, ‘Well, I’d like to go.’ And she said, ‘Well, come on, then,’” he says, his smile widening. “We made lunch, and…”

His voice trails off, and he recognizes a local walking a dog on the street. He shakes his friend’s hand while the dog sniffs around at our feet.

“Did I tell you I got my eyes on a ton of elk on 66?” the guy asks.

“Nice,” Jeff says. He mentions the upcoming fall hunting season. It’s not the same, but he’ll still go. Jennifer would always accompany him on those trips; she’d camp or hike while he went out looking for elk, but now Jeff mostly spends his time alone in the mountains. He still goes out to scavenge for sheds, something Jennifer loved to do, and when he found a trove of horns earlier this year, he was convinced she was looking out for him.

A few months after Jennifer died, Jeff drove alone to California to try and find himself. He camped along the way and wondered if he should start a new life somewhere west of Ridgway, somewhere he hadn’t lost two wives in the span of a decade. Losing one to cancer and another to a sudden hiking accident were both painful but altogether different traumatic experiences. At least with Dawn, he could explain how it had happened. With Jennifer, he couldn’t. “It still doesn’t make any sense to me,” he says.

Jeff eventually decided to return to Ridgway, to try and begin again in a place where he had friends and jobs where the locals relied on him. He mustered the strength to call each of the clients that Jennifer had pet-sat for to let them know what had happened to his wife, even though he couldn’t fully explain it. He removed memories of Jennifer in the house, her clothes and most of their photos together, because some days life could feel unbearable when he looked at those reminders. But she was never far from his mind, and he found some peace when he joined Jennifer’s adult son, Anthony, on a hike up to Mount Abrams, a 12,000-foot peak in the San Juans, to spread her ashes last summer.

Before Jeff heads back to work, he shares with me where the mine is located, because a few months earlier, he had gone up to see it for the first and only time himself. “I went up there thinking, you know, maybe I’ll find some answers,” he tells me a few weeks later, after learning that the shaft has been covered. He didn’t plan to go back, so that day he saw the mine was how he will always remember it.

He took Mia with him, and together they followed coordinates up the trail that had been given to Jeff by a search and rescue volunteer who had looked for Jennifer. He still had a hard time finding it. He asked a few hikers on the trail if they might know where it was, but they didn’t. After a while, he realized he had walked right past it, just as he did that fateful night, when he ran up the mountain screaming Jennifer’s name, hoping he might hear her cries for help.

When he doubled back down the trail, he finally spotted the black mesh fence in the trees, and he hiked up the slope. Mia went with him, but it didn’t appear that she remembered the place. Jeff walked around the perimeter of the fence, staring at the open shaft, before sitting down on the forest floor. He stayed there for more than an hour, talking to Jennifer and asking her questions.

There were no answers. Jeff finally left the hill with Mia and trudged back across the trail to his truck. He drove down the Million Dollar Highway and into Ridgway, no closer to understanding how Jennifer ended up in that mine.

#8273. Top 10 Resorts in the East for Snow Quality (2027)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

On the East Coast, skiing is about more than great lines and great snow. It’s SUVs trudging through storms with their ski racks, salt stains, and “SKI THE EAST” bumper stickers. The snow is firmer, the peaks are lower, and terrain is more dense, but no less breathtaking. Mostly, though, it’s about skiing not as a hobby but as an identity—something you do because you’ve always done it, and always done it here.

Maybe you’ve heard that the East Coast has a reputation for its “ice.” For much of the region, that’s an outdated stereotype. Sure, these spots might not get the massive powder days that some of the Western resorts are known for, but with modern innovations in snowmaking (and a few good breaks from Mother Nature), the East can more than hold its own. After all, anyone in their right mind would have chosen and East Coast winter over the West’s sad season last year.

If you’re looking for the East Coast resorts that typically get the best snow, the 10 resorts listed below are a fine place to begin. These choices, which come from SKI’s Annual Reader Resort Survey, are known for serving up the most powder days and the best snow conditions all season long.

#8272. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Early into the second night of the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

“I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He said, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

“We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll said. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was big: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

“I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”

Yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle says he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”
